newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week- Longs to ride likely rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week- Longs to ride likely rate rise.

text.p: UK gilts have to negotiate their way around plenty of economic data, a key decision on interest rates and news on supply this week, but analysts believe the market will emerge unscathed.

"Overall, the fundamentals are looking very favourable for gilts," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "With the spread against Bunds at around 155 at the 10 year area, there is probably some value there."

The market will be looking at a big decline in May manufacturing output data released Monday and June retail prices on Tuesday for an indication of how the Bank of England will set interest rates, analysts said.

The Bank of England's monetary policy committee, recently empowered by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown to set interest rates, convenes later this week with an announcement due at midday on Thursday.
The market will also be looking for an indication of future gilt supply with an announcement of the auction schedule for the third quarter expected on Friday.
After a downward revision to public sector debt forecasts in the budget, the Bank of England only has to sell a further 16.5 billion stg in this financial year. Last year, it sold nearly 40 billion.
Many analysts felt last Wednesday's budget did not go far enough to stem buoyant domestic consumer demand and see a rate rise as inevitable.
Steve Scott, bond analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, reflected the market view by forecasting a 25 basis point rise. "No more than 25...which is priced in," he said.
"Fifty would smack of panic which would send the wrong message to the market that there was something to panic about in the UK economy."

Coleman said that, even if there were an unexpected 50 basis point rise, which would be overkill in his mind, gilts would bounce back from the initial shock because the implications for inflation would be good.

Scott pointed to the weaker than expected British manufacturing output, which fell 1.1 percent in May -- the biggest fall since 1993 -- and a fall in industrial production of 0.1 percent on the month as an indication of low inflationary pressures.
"With inflation figures still relatively low there is no reason to send panic signals to the market."

Analysts expected underlying June retail price inflation to be in line with current levels at 2.5 percent year-on-year. "We are forecasting around 1.9 by the end of the year, but our forecast for June is stable at around 2.5 for this month," Scott said.
He said the market would be keeping an eye on the breakdown of clothing and household goods to see for any discounting ahead of the summer sales.
Phillip Tyson, analyst at HSBC Markets, said that while the arguments for monetary tightening were strong, the strength of sterling would dampen additional hikes.

"Near term, the gilt market's disappointment with Brown's budget is set to fade," he said. "Although sentiment has been undermined by worries about consumer spending and higher base rates, the outlook for the fiscal position is looking increasingly encouraging."

The pound has leapt around 20 percent since last August, a factor which is crippling exporters and is set to hit Britain's terms of trade as strong domestic demand sucks in cheap imports while exporters struggle with higher prices.
The short end of the gilt curve would still suffer from near term interest rate rise fears, but the longer end of the curve is set to continue last week's healthy gains, analysts said.

"The curve is now virtually flat between two-10 years as interest rate worries have put upward pressure on the short yields, while the longs have been much more resilient given supply/inflation arguments," said Tyson.
"The curve will invert even further as the short end suffers relative to the long end," Coleman added.
September short sterling was discounting base rates at about seven percent by the end of the third quarter. It stood at 92.88 by 1200 GMT. Base rates are now 6.5 percent

"We have the PSBR coming down and the prospect of reduced supply next year, in addition we are likely to see a modest increase in interest rates which will reassure the markets that inflation is under control," Coleman said.
"On balance, the outlook for gilts is pretty good," he said. -- London Newsroom, + 44 171 542 7708
